## Proof

**Claim:** Yes, $f$ and $g$ necessarily agree everywhere.

Let $D = \{x \in \mathbb{R} : f(x) \neq g(x)\}$. By hypothesis $D$ has Lebesgue measure zero, i.e. $m(D) = 0$.

Fix an arbitrary point $x \in \mathbb{R}$. We show $f(x) = g(x)$.

For each $n \geq 1$, consider the interval $I_n = (x - \tfrac{1}{n},\, x)$. Since $m(D) = 0$, the set $D \cap I_n$ has measure zero, and in particular $I_n \setminus D$ is nonempty (indeed of full measure in $I_n$). Choose a point
$$y_n \in I_n \setminus D, \qquad \text{so that } x - \tfrac{1}{n} < y_n < x \text{ and } f(y_n) = g(y_n).$$

Then $y_n \to x$ from the left. Using left-continuity of $f$ at $x$,
$$f(x) = \lim_{n \to \infty} f(y_n).$$
Using (left) continuity of $g$ at $x$,
$$g(x) = \lim_{n \to \infty} g(y_n).$$
But $f(y_n) = g(y_n)$ for every $n$ by construction, so the two limits coincide:
$$f(x) = \lim_{n\to\infty} f(y_n) = \lim_{n\to\infty} g(y_n) = g(x).$$

Since $x$ was arbitrary, $f(x) = g(x)$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$.

**Remark on the hypotheses.** The argument uses only that $f$ is left-continuous and that $g$ is left-continuous (full continuity of $g$ is more than enough). The measure-zero set $D$ cannot block every left-approaching sequence, because any interval $(x-\varepsilon, x)$ has positive measure and hence contains points outside $D$. Thus the values of $f$ to the left of $x$ — which determine $f(x)$ by left-continuity — coincide with the values of $g$ there, and continuity of $g$ pins those values to $g(x)$.

### PROOF COMPLETE
